verses.text: This was the lot for the tribe of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. As for Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, because he was a man of war, therefore he had Gilead and Bashan.

So this was for the rest of the children of Manasseh according to their families: for the children of Abiezer, for the children of Helek, for the children of Asriel, for the children of Shechem, for the children of Hepher, and for the children of Shemida. These were the male children of Manasseh the son of Joseph according to their families.

But Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, had no sons, but daughters. These are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.

They came to Eleazar the priest, and to Joshua the son of Nun, and to the princes, saying, “Yahweh commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers.” Therefore according to the commandment of Yahweh he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father.
Ten parts fell to Manasseh, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is beyond the Jordan;
because the daughters of Manasseh had an inheritance among his sons. The land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the sons of Manasseh.
The border of Manasseh was from Asher to Michmethath, which is before Shechem. The border went along to the right hand, to the inhabitants of En Tappuah.
The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh; but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the children of Ephraim.

The border went down to the brook of Kanah, southward of the brook. These cities belonged to Ephraim among the cities of Manasseh. The border of Manasseh was on the north side of the brook, and ended at the sea.
Southward it was Ephraim’s, and northward it was Manasseh’s, and the sea was his border. They reached to Asher on the north, and to Issachar on the east.

Manasseh had three heights in Issachar, in Asher Beth Shean and its towns, and Ibleam and its towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and its towns, and the inhabitants of Endor and its towns, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its towns, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its towns.
Yet the children of Manasseh couldn’t drive out the inhabitants of those cities; but the Canaanites would dwell in that land.
When the children of Israel had grown strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, and didn’t utterly drive them out.
The children of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, “Why have you given me just one lot and one part for an inheritance, since we are a numerous people, because Yahweh has blessed us so far?”

Joshua said to them, “If you are a numerous people, go up to the forest, and clear land for yourself there in the land of the Perizzites and of the Rephaim; since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you.”

The children of Joseph said, “The hill country is not enough for us. All the Canaanites who dwell in the land of the valley have chariots of iron, both those who are in Beth Shean and its towns, and those who are in the valley of Jezreel.”
Joshua spoke to the house of Joseph, that is, to Ephraim and to Manasseh, saying, “You are a numerous people, and have great power. You shall not have one lot only;

but the hill country shall be yours. Although it is a forest, you shall cut it down, and it’s farthest extent shall be yours; for you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong.”

footnotes.content: Manasseh gets the first claim as Joseph's eldest. That's how inheritance worked—the firstborn led, the warlike Machir especially. But notice: the land comes with conditions, with enemies still dwelling there. A blessed share and a fight ahead, both at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lots are divided by family clans—Abiezer, Helek, Shechem, and the rest. Each name matters because each family mattered to the Lord's eye. This is how grace parcels out: not mass distribution, but family by family, known.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zelophehad had no sons, only daughters. In that culture, that meant nothing—until five women walked up and asked for what was theirs. The Lord had already prepared their hearts to speak, and the law was ready to hear them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These daughters came to Eleazar and Joshua with a claim grounded in the Lord's own word: "Yahweh commanded Moses to give us an inheritance." They didn't plead or apologize. They simply spoke truth. And the leaders—to their credit—listened and obeyed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten portions came to Manasseh—a generous lot. But the text keeps reminding us: *besides* Gilead and Bashan, *across* the Jordan. The blessing is good, but it's split and stretched. The full promise takes more faith to receive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The daughters received their share among the sons—a quiet revolution in justice. Zelophehad's family line lives on through women because the Lord saw their faithfulness and honored it. Grace doesn't always follow custom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The border runs from Asher to Michmethath, near Shechem—places with their own stories of God's dealings. A map is also a history book if you read it with remembrance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tappuah sits between two tribes—Manasseh's and Ephraim's. Some possessions are shared or contested. The Lord permits this, and it teaches us: not everything comes without friction. Some blessings demand we learn to dwell peaceably with neighbors.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The border goes down to the Kanah brook—a boundary that divides brothers. Ephraim and Manasseh, both Joseph's line, both blessed, but marked apart. The Lord's gifts sometimes create firm lines between neighbors so each can inherit fully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephraim south, Manasseh north, the sea their western wall. Each tribe has a place, a boundary, a clear inheritance. When the Lord divides, He divides with precision. Each family knows what is theirs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Manasseh receives Beth Shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach, Megiddo—cities with names and stories. These aren't abstractions. A rich land with towers and wells and streets full of people who need the Lord just as much as we do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Manasseh couldn't drive out the Canaanites. They *couldn't*—not "didn't try" or "chose not to." This is where the text gets honest: promised land doesn't mean empty land. Faith meets resistance, and we live in the tension.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor instead of driving them out entirely. Not the cleanest victory, but a practical one. Sometimes the Lord allows compromise in tactics while keeping His promise intact.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph's sons speak up: "Why just one lot? We are numerous. We are blessed!" There's a boldness here—not quite complaint, but a question. They want more. The Lord permits us to ask, to want, even to advocate for ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua tells them to go to the forest and clear land themselves—in the territory of the Perizzites and Rephaim. He's not dismissing them; he's inviting them to act, to claim what they need through their own hands and courage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The hill country is not enough, but the valley is too strong—iron chariots!" They see the problem before them: the high ground is tight, the low ground is defended. It's a real fear, not a spiritual excuse. The Lord hears honest struggles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua answers: "You are strong and numerous. Take the hill country, clear the forest, and you shall drive out the Canaanites—yes, even with iron chariots." Readers today hear an echo: sometimes our fear of obstacles is bigger than the obstacles themselves, and the Lord calls us to act in faith past the fear, trusting His power to make the rough places smooth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
